name: Software Engineering
tagline: Highest ceiling, longest runway, hardest current job market for juniors.
description: Self-taught developers are real and there are a lot of them. The catch is timing: the junior developer market tightened significantly after 2023 and has not fully recovered, so the honest expectation is 12–24 months of study plus a genuinely competitive portfolio. If you want the fastest route to any tech job, this is not it. If you want the highest long-term ceiling and you enjoy building things, it is.

salaryRange.note: Junior developer range in most US markets; $50Ks in low cost-of-living areas and at small agencies, higher in major tech metros. BLS reports a $133,080 median for software developers (May 2024) — that reflects experienced engineers, not first jobs.

remoteFriendly.note: The field is remote-friendly overall, but junior roles are the least remote tier — companies want new developers where they can be mentored. Expect the first job to be hybrid or on-site more often than not, then remote afterward.

realityCheck: 'Learn to code in 6 months and get a $100K job' was true for a window around 2015–2021 and is not true now. Plan on a year-plus, expect a long application grind, and treat the first offer as the goal rather than the salary. The people who succeed build things continuously instead of collecting courses.
whyItFits: If you like the puzzle more than the paycheck — if you'd tinker with this anyway — you'll outlast the people who are here for the salary. That persistence is the actual differentiator, because the technical material is all freely available.
nextRoles: Application Support Engineer (a common side door)

motivation.quote: Nobody asked to see my degree. They asked what I'd built, and then they asked me to build something in front of them.
motivation.story: The self-taught developers who make it share a boring pattern: they built things constantly and in public. Not one portfolio project rushed at the end — a GitHub profile with two years of commits, a couple of real applications other people actually use, and open-source contributions. The portfolio is not a formality at the end of the path; it *is* the path.
motivation.source: Composite of the pattern described across r/learnprogramming and freeCodeCamp community success stories

interviewPrep.question: Given a string, return the first non-repeating character.
interviewPrep.why: A typical junior screening problem. Practice talking while you code — interviewers score your reasoning, not just the answer. A hash map counting pass then a second scan is the expected solution.

interviewPrep.question: What's the difference between an array and a hash map, and when would you use each?
interviewPrep.why: Data structure basics come up in nearly every junior interview. Arrays: ordered, index access, O(n) search. Hash maps: key lookup in O(1), unordered.

interviewPrep.question: What happens when you submit a form on a web page?
interviewPrep.why: Tests whether you understand the request/response cycle, HTTP methods, validation on client vs. server, and what the server does with the data.

interviewPrep.question: You committed a bug to main. What do you do?
interviewPrep.why: They want to see that you know revert vs. reset, and that your instinct is to communicate rather than quietly force-push over history.

interviewPrep.question: Walk me through the hardest bug you've fixed in your own project.
interviewPrep.why: The most important question for a self-taught candidate. Have a specific, technical, honest story: symptom, hypotheses, how you narrowed it down, the fix, what you'd do differently.

interviewPrep.question: Write a SQL query joining two tables and filtering the results.
interviewPrep.why: Almost every application job touches a database. Know INNER vs LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY, and WHERE vs HAVING.

interviewPrep.question: How do you handle a code review that rejects your approach?
interviewPrep.why: Juniors are hired on coachability. Answer: ask what the concern is, understand the reasoning, change the code, don't take it personally.

steps.title: Learn programming fundamentals in one language
steps.description: Pick one language and stay with it for at least six months. JavaScript (fastest route to visible, shareable projects) or Python (cleaner syntax, opens data and automation work) are both correct choices; switching languages every month is the mistake. Learn variables, control flow, functions, data structures, and error handling until they're automatic.
steps.costNote: Free. The best beginner programming curricula in existence cost nothing.
steps.outcome: You can write, run, and debug a program of a few hundred lines without a tutorial.

resources.name: The Odin Project (free full-stack curriculum)
resources.notes: Free, project-based, and widely considered the best free path to employability. Requires a real computer for most of it.

resources.name: freeCodeCamp
resources.notes: Free, browser-based — which means it works on a library computer or even a phone in a pinch. Certifications included at no cost.

resources.name: CS50x — Harvard's Introduction to Computer Science
resources.notes: Free to audit including all assignments (paid certificate optional). The best free explanation of how computers actually work under your code.

resources.name: Exercism (free mentored practice)
resources.notes: Free coding exercises with volunteer human code review — unusually valuable for a self-taught learner.

steps.title: Learn Git and GitHub properly
steps.description: Version control is not optional and it is tested. Learn branching, merging, pull requests, resolving conflicts, and writing commit messages a stranger can read. Push everything you write from day one — a GitHub profile with two years of history is one of the strongest signals a self-taught candidate can produce, and you can only build it by starting early.
steps.costNote: Free. GitHub's free tier covers everything you need including private repos and Pages hosting.
steps.outcome: A GitHub profile with real, regular commits.
steps.resumeBullet: Proficient with Git and GitHub: branching strategies, pull request workflow, code review, and conflict resolution.

resources.name: GitHub Skills (free interactive courses)
resources.notes: Free official interactive tutorials.

resources.name: Learn Git Branching (free visual tutorial)
resources.notes: Free. The clearest way to build a mental model of branches and merges.

resources.name: Pro Git book (free, official)
resources.notes: Free online. Reference rather than a tutorial.

steps.title: Build the web fundamentals: HTML, CSS, and the DOM
steps.description: Even backend developers need this. Semantic HTML, the CSS box model, flexbox and grid, responsive design, and how JavaScript manipulates the DOM. Build several small static pages from scratch — no frameworks, no templates — until layout stops feeling like guesswork.
steps.outcome: You can build a responsive page from a design without copying a template.
steps.resumeBullet: Built responsive, accessible web interfaces with semantic HTML, CSS (flexbox/grid), and vanilla JavaScript.

resources.name: MDN Web Docs — Learn Web Development
resources.notes: Free. The authoritative web reference and a genuinely good tutorial track.

resources.name: CSS Diner / Flexbox Froggy / Grid Garden (free CSS games)
resources.notes: Free browser games. Work fine on a phone and make CSS layout stick faster than reading does.

resources.name: Frontend Mentor (free design challenges)
resources.notes: Free tier with real designs to implement — turns 'what do I build?' into a solved problem.

steps.title: Learn a framework and how to talk to a database
steps.description: React remains the most job-dense frontend framework; on the backend, Node/Express or Python/Django are both safe bets. Pair it with SQL and one database (PostgreSQL is the best default). The combination — frontend framework, backend API, real database — is what 'full-stack junior' means on a job posting.
steps.costNote: Free. Official docs for React, Express, Django, and PostgreSQL are all free and are better than most paid courses.
steps.outcome: You can build and deploy an application with a UI, an API, and persistent data.
steps.resumeBullet: Developed full-stack applications with React, a Node/Express (or Django) REST API, and PostgreSQL, including authentication and relational data modeling.

resources.name: React official documentation and tutorial
resources.notes: Free. The rewritten docs are excellent — start here rather than with a paid course.

resources.name: Full Stack Open (University of Helsinki, free)
resources.notes: Free, university-quality React/Node/GraphQL curriculum with real depth. One of the strongest free resources anywhere.

resources.name: PostgreSQL Tutorial
resources.notes: Free SQL and PostgreSQL fundamentals.

resources.name: Django official tutorial
resources.notes: Free. The Python-side alternative to Node/Express.

steps.title: Build three real projects — not tutorial clones
steps.description: Three deployed applications that solve actual problems, ideally for actual people. A to-do app and a weather widget will not distinguish you; a scheduling tool your cousin's landscaping business uses will. Each project needs: a live URL, a public repo, a README explaining the problem and the architecture, and tests. Depth beats quantity — three good ones beat ten shallow ones.
steps.costNote: Free. Vercel, Netlify, Render, and Fly.io all have free tiers sufficient for portfolio projects. A custom domain (~$12/year) is a nice touch but optional.
steps.outcome: Three deployed, documented applications with public source code.
steps.resumeBullet: Designed, built, and deployed three production web applications (React/Node/PostgreSQL) with authentication, REST APIs, automated tests, and CI/CD — used by real users.

resources.name: Vercel free tier
resources.notes: Free hosting for frontend and serverless projects.

resources.name: Render free tier
resources.notes: Free tier for web services and PostgreSQL, with the caveat that free instances sleep when idle.

resources.name: app-ideas repository (project inspiration)
resources.notes: Free. Use it for structure, but prefer problems you or people you know actually have.

steps.title: Contribute to open source
steps.description: Open source contributions solve the 'no professional experience' problem more directly than any personal project, because they show you can read someone else's codebase, follow their conventions, and survive code review. Start with documentation fixes and small bugs in projects you actually use. Getting one PR merged into a real project is worth more than a month of tutorials.
steps.outcome: Merged pull requests in projects you didn't write.
steps.resumeBullet: Contributed to open-source projects: submitted and shipped pull requests addressing bugs and documentation gaps, working within existing codebases and review processes.

resources.name: Good First Issue
resources.notes: Free. Aggregates beginner-friendly issues across projects.

resources.name: First Contributions (guided walkthrough)
resources.notes: Free. A practice repo for making your first pull request without fear.

resources.name: Hacktoberfest (annual, October)
resources.notes: Free. A once-a-year excuse to make contributions with a lot of community support around it.

steps.title: Practice interview problems and system design basics
steps.description: Technical interviews are their own skill, separate from building software. Do 60–100 easy and medium problems on a platform like LeetCode — enough to be fluent, not enough to become a full-time competitive programmer. Learn to narrate your reasoning aloud, because silent correct answers score worse than spoken imperfect ones.
steps.costNote: Free. LeetCode's free tier and NeetCode's free curated lists are enough; premium tiers are optional.
steps.outcome: You can solve and explain a medium-difficulty problem under time pressure.

resources.name: NeetCode 150 (free curated problem list)
resources.notes: Free. Structured by pattern rather than random difficulty — far more efficient than grinding at random.

resources.name: LeetCode
resources.notes: Free tier is sufficient. Premium (~$35/month) is not necessary for junior roles.

resources.name: Pramp / free peer mock interviews
resources.notes: Free peer-to-peer mock interviews. Uncomfortable and extremely effective.

steps.title: Apply strategically — including through side doors
steps.description: The direct route (apply to 'Junior Developer' postings) is the most crowded one. Side doors work better: application support engineer, QA with automation, internal tools developer, technical support at a software company with a stated path into engineering, or a small non-tech business that needs its one developer. Also apply to apprenticeship programs — several large companies run them specifically for non-degree candidates.
steps.costNote: Free. Never pay for a bootcamp that promises job placement in exchange for an income share agreement without reading the terms very carefully.

resources.name: r/cscareerquestions
resources.notes: Free. Skew pessimistic, but useful for calibrating the current junior market.

resources.name: Hacker News 'Who is Hiring' monthly threads
resources.notes: Free. Posted the first working day of each month. Smaller companies, less resume screening, more willingness to hire on portfolio.

resources.name: Apprenticeship programs (search: 'software apprenticeship no degree')
resources.notes: Free. US Department of Labor apprenticeship finder — registered tech apprenticeships pay while you train and don't require a degree.
